division.heading: Lawyers’ Charges, Retainer Agreements and Right of Review

operative_text.controlling:
10.20(1)  The Court, on application by a party with notice to the
other party, may direct a decision of a review officer to be entered
as a judgment or order.
(2)  No direction may be made under subrule (1) before the time for
an appeal of the review officer’s decision has expired or, if the
decision is being appealed, before a decision is made under rule
10.27.

BOOK_A.title: Enforcement of Review Ofﬁcer’s Decision
BOOK_A.commentary:
Now R.10.20(1) requires an application in order to have a review ofﬁcer's decision be made
an order or judgment. The March 2020, R.10.20 amendment requires advance notice to the other
party. Where the order was made in June 2018 and the time to appeal it ran out before the Rule
change, the new requirement for notice did not apply.¹
An Applications Judge cannot refuse a R.10.20 application for execution (enforcement) on a
legal account if a King's Bench justice (on appeal from the review ofﬁcer) has already held liability
established (a conﬁrmed amount).²
Once the two-year limitation period to sue in contract has expired, a lawyer cannot seek leave
to enforce a certiﬁcate.³
The interaction of a belated appeal from taxation (review) of fees, and a challenge later to the
retainer, is discussed.⁴

footnotes.text: The person ordered to pay had had notice of the review application itself, however, and was personally present at it, and he raised no objections though then asked if there were any other issues. He gave no useful evidence about why he did not try to appeal or open the matter up earlier: Gowling v. Tsybulnyk 2020 ABQB 479, JCC 1701 16757 (Aug 20).

Snyder & Assoc. v. Brown (M) 2005 ABQB 59. Taxation of a law ﬁrm’s account to its client was to be enforced, after another judge had found a proper retainer. He had not granted a judgment, but this judge did. There were no more issues to decide: McCuaig Desrochers v. Zivkovic 2006 ABQB 366, 399 AR 300.
Macleod Dixon v. Fazal (M) 2003 ABQB 744, 336 AR 198, affd 2004 ABQB 523, 30 Alta LR(4th) 202. On limitations issues, see R.10.11n.

BOOK_B.title: Enforcement of review officer's decision

commentary.text: Rule 10.20 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.20. 1. Filing Statement of Claim Not Necessary This rule gives the court a discretion to order the enforcement of a solicitor's taxed bill of costs as a judgment of the court. In this respect, I entirely agree with the decision of the master in chambers. Nothing in this rule requires the commencement of an action by way of statement of claim before the granting of an enforcement order. This issue was decided in Griffiths v. Hughes (1847), 16 M. & W. 809 … I have found not subsequent authority to the contrary. Rusnak v. A.C.H.A.I.A. Holdings Ltd. (1983), 28 Alta. L.R. (2d) 187 (Q.B.), at 188, per McFadyen J. 2. Master Has Jurisdiction under Rule There remains to be considered only the issue of whether the exercise of the power conferred by R. 651 is a power reserved to a judge appointed pursuant to s. 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867. To determine this issue, it is necessary to consider the tests set out by Dickson J. in Re Residential Tenancies Act of Ont., [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 … While the power granted by R. 651(2) may historically have been a power granted to a Superior Court Judge and was a power which was exercised only by a Superior Court Judge at the time of Confederation, I am satisfied that the power now cannot be considered a “judicial function” as that term is defined with Dickson J. at p. 571 where he states: Step two involves consideration of the function within its institutional setting to determine whether the function itself is different when viewed in that setting. In particular, can the function still be considered to be a ‘judicial’ function? In addressing the issue it is important to keep in mind the further statement by Rand J. in Dupont v. Inglis, [1958] S.C.R. 535, 14 D.L.R. (2d) 417 at 424, that ‘it is the subject-matter rather than the apparatus of adjudication that is determinative’. Thus the question of whether any particular function is ‘judicial’ is not to be determined simply on the basis of procedural trappings. The primary issue is the nature of the question which the tribunal is called upon to decide. Where the tribunal is faced with a private dispute between parties, and is called upon to adjudicate through the application of a recognized body of rules in a manner consistent with fairness and impartiality, then, normally, it is acting in a ‘judicial capacity’. To borrow the terminology of Professor Ronald Dworkin, the judicial task involves questions of ‘principle’, that is, consideration of the competing rights of individuals or groups. This can be contrasted with questions of ‘policy’ involving competing views of the collective good of the community as a whole: see Dworkin, Taking Rights Seriously (1977), at pp. 82–90 (Duckworth). In exercising the discretion granted by R. 651(2) the master is not adjudicating on the dispute between two parties or on competing rights or claims of two parties. The function of the master is to ensure that the person against whom the order is sought was in fact served with a notice of taxation and that the certificate of taxation is in the proper form and to ensure that all outstanding issues between the parties have been resolved … It is clear that the taxation certificate is final and conclusive as to amounts mentioned against parties served with the notice of taxation. The rules do not purport to authorize the master to resolve finally and conclusively all issues which may arise between the solicitor and the named defendants respecting the account and the liability to pay that account. Most other issues may be decided on a reference by the taxation officer to the judge of the court. However, where any issues remain unresolved, the application under R. 651(2) should either be rejected and the solicitor left to his remedy to bring an action by way of statement of claim or there should be a direction that the unresolved issue be tried. As a result, I reach the conclusion that the function of the master is not a judicial function as that term is defined by Dickson J. I am satisfied that the master had jurisdiction to deal with the application made pursuant to R. 651(2). Rusnak v. A.C.H.A.I.A. Holdings Ltd. (1983), 28 Alta. L.R. (2d) 187 (Q.B.), at 190–91, per McFadyen J. 3. Prior Determination of Liability Required Where there is a dispute about liability an order under Rule 651(2) is not appropriate until the issue of liability is resolved. That depends on the terms of the agreement, if any, between the client and the solicitors. The application for an order under Rule 651(2) is adjourned pending disposition of the main issue between the parties. Peterson, Ross v. Kirkwood (1984), 52 A.R. 284 (Master), at 293, per Master Funduk, quoting Gilbert v. Douglas Rentals Ltd. (26th July 1983), Edmonton 8303-15325 (Q.B.) (unreported)). In Shreem Holdings Inc. v. Barr Picard, 2013 ABQB 257, 2013 CarswellAlta 540, 560 A.R. 272, 88 Alta. L.R. (5th) 359, 49 C.P.C. (7th) 419, Justice Wakeling said, at paragraphs 25–28, 30–33, and 40: 25 Rule 10.20(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court states that “[t]he Court may direct a decision of a review officer to be entered as a judgment or order”. 26 A judgment is “a decision made by the court upon the respective claims and rights of the parties to a proceeding”. L. Abrams & K. McGuiness, Canadian Civil Procedure Law 1358 (2d ed. 2010). It resolves a dispute and is capable of enforcement. See Bozson v. Altrincham Urban District Council, [1903] 1 K.B. 547, 548 (C.A) (a judgment reflects the final disposition of the “rights of the parties”); 16(2) Halsbury's Law of England 429 (4th ed. reissue (2003) (a judgment in personam determines “the rights of parties as between one another”) & 2 W. Williston & R. Rolls, The Law of Civil Procedure 1020 (1970) (“Decisions which finally determine the … questions at issue in an action inter partes are judgments”. 27 This court should not exercise its discretion in favour of a rule 10.20(1) applicant if the certificate of review, read as a whole, does not resolve a dispute between a client and a lawyer. 28 No purpose is served by giving a certificate of review the status of a judgment when it can never be enforced. That is the sole rationale of rule 10.20(1). See Griffith v. Hughes, 153 E.R. 1418 (Ex. 1847). … 30 A review officer who conducts a review of a lawyer's charges has a limited jurisdiction under the Alberta Rules of Court. This is the case with respect to both procedural and substantive matters. 31 Significant substantive limitations restrict the questions the review officer may resolve. According to rule 10.19(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court, a review officer “may … allow the [lawyer] charges, or vary, reduce or disallow all or any of the charges and certify the amount payable for and against each party”. The rules even dictate the factors the review officer must take into account in arriving at a reasonable charge. Alberta Rules of Court, rule 10.19(1). 32 A review officer may not make any substantive decision not listed in rule 10.19(3). 33 It follows that a review officer may not determine if a solicitor-client relationship exists. Gilbert v. Douglas Rentals Ltd., [1983] A.J. No. 664, Edmonton Q.B. 8303-15325 (Master July 26, 1983) (“Like any other contract a dispute about the terms must be resolved by a judicial officer”). Nor may the review officer adjudicate a claim that the lawyer agreed to accept a fixed fee. Rusnak v. Commodity Investors Syndicate of Canada Ltd., 48 A.R. 311, 315 (Q. B 1982) (a taxing officer could not hear client's claim that the lawyer had agreed to a fixed fee). The review officer is also sailing in prohibited water if he settles the amount a client had paid towards an account. … 40 A court should not accord the status of a judgment to a review officer's certificate of review which reveals that there is a dispute as to who the client is and the amount the client owes the lawyer. Gibson v. Bassie, Kantor & Plupek[1985] 2 A.U.D. 923, 924 (C.A.) (a court may enforce a taxation certificate “as a judgment … unless the terms of the retainer are disputed”); Rusnak and Savaryn v. A.C.H.A.I.A. Holdings Ltd., 51 A.R. 196, 201 (Q.B. 1983) (a taxation certificate should not be entered by court order as a judgment “where a substantial issue exists as to the liability of the defendant or any one of them”); Peterson, Ross v. Kirwood, 52 A.R. 284, 292 (Master 1984) (“As the taxing officer has no jurisdiction to decide liability it would be illogical to hold his certificate prevents a client … from disputing liability); Field and Field v. Hys, 101 A.R. 31, 34 (Master 1989) (taxation certificate not enforced because alleged clients denied they were responsible for the account); Brian A. Beresh Professional Corporation v. Schneider, 106 A.R. 251, 293 (Master 1990) (taxation certificate not enforced as if it were a judgment because the husband denied he was responsible for his wife's legal fees); Gilbert v. Douglas Rentals Ltd., Edmonton Q.B. 8303-15325 (Master July 26, 1983) (“where there is a dispute about liability an order under Rule 651(2) is not appropriate until the issue of liability is resolved”) &Rusnak v. Commodity Investors Syndicate of Canada Ltd., 48 A.R. 311, 315–16 (Q.B 1982) (the court refused to enforce a taxing officer's assessment because there was a dispute about the existence of a fixed fee). 4. Client May Obtain Judgment for Overpayment In Welsh v. Jones (1998), 60 Alta. L.R. (3d) 331 (Master), a lawyer rendered an account for professional services, and it was paid by the client. However, the client taxed the account and it was reduced by $1,800. The lawyer did not repay the overpayment. The client applied to have the overpayment enforced against the lawyer (who had subsequently left the practice of law). In allowing the client's application, Master Alberstat, at p. 332, said: The rule under which lawyers apply to have their taxed bills enforced as judgments seems to apply only to lawyers taxing a bill. In any event that is how it has been interpreted and treated by practise [sic] and usage. The question is whether a client can avail him or herself of the same rule? Rule 4 says: As to all matters not provided for in the Rules the practice as far as may be shall be regulated by analogy thereto. The respondent argues that there is a provision provided for by [sic] the client and that is to sue for the amount taxed down. I reject that argument. A lawyer may tax a bill either before or after payment although usually the taxation is prior to payment. A client may tax a bill of a lawyer either before or after payment. If the bill is taxed prior to payment the lawyer may then apply under rule 651, to have the taxation enforced as a judgment. If a bill is taxed after it is paid, and is taxed down, the payment is an overpayment. The person having made the payment is entitled to be repaid the amount overpaid. If a lawyer can have an unpaid taxed bill enforced as a judgment pursuant to rule 651 then why can not a client have the overpayment enforced as a judgment? I cannot see why that should not be the case applying rule 4.

BOOK_C.title: Enforcement of review officer’s decision

commentary.text:
Rule 10.20 specifically contemplates that a judgment is a step that follows the certificate of review. Felesky Flynn LLP v. SCL Engineering Ltd., [2013] A.J. No. 60, 2013 ABPC 10 at para. 28 (Alta. Prov. Ct.). . The decision of the review officer does not vest a new cause of action in the plaintiff, but rather is a vehicle to be used by the lawyer within the confines of Part 10 of the to obtain a judgment.
Alberta Rules of Court
